lessons.title: Grammar: There is/are and prepositions of place

items.headword: There is / there are and prepositions of place
items.definition: how to say what exists somewhere and where things are located
items.explanationTR:
We use there is with singular and uncountable nouns, and there are with plural nouns, to say that something exists in a place.
• There is a small park behind our building.
• There are two bathrooms in this apartment.
The negative is there isn't / there aren't, and questions start with Is there...? / Are there...?
• There isn't an elevator, only stairs.
• Are there any shops near your street?
Prepositions of place tell us exactly where something is.
• in / on / at – The keys are on the table. The milk is in the fridge. She's at home.
• next to / between – The bakery is next to the bank. The cafe is between the bakery and the park.
• in front of / behind – There's a bike in front of the door.
• under / above – The cat is sleeping under the bed.
Combine both structures to describe a home or a neighborhood clearly: There is a bus stop in front of our building, and there are two supermarkets between our street and the park.

questions.prompt: ---- a small supermarket at the end of our street.
questions.explanationTR: 'Supermarket' is singular, so the sentence needs 'There is'; 'There are' is used for plural nouns, and 'There has' and 'There be' are not correct forms.

questions.prompt: ---- many old trees in this neighborhood.
questions.explanationTR: 'Trees' is plural, so the sentence needs 'There are'; 'There is' and 'There was' do not agree with a plural noun.

questions.prompt: There ---- a small yard behind the house, but there isn't a garage.
questions.explanationTR: 'Yard' is singular, so 'is' is correct after 'There'; 'are' would need a plural noun, and 'be'/'has'/'having' are not correct here.

questions.prompt: Your keys are ---- the kitchen table, next to the fruit bowl.
questions.explanationTR: 'On' is used for something resting on top of a flat surface like a table; keys 'under' or 'behind' the table could not be next to the fruit bowl.

questions.prompt: Our apartment is ---- the bakery and the pharmacy.
questions.explanationTR: 'Between' is used when something has one thing on each side, here the bakery and the pharmacy; 'next to' only mentions one neighboring place.

questions.prompt: There's a big lamp ---- the dining table; it hangs from the ceiling.
questions.explanationTR: 'Above' means higher than something without touching it, like a lamp that hangs from the ceiling over a table; 'on' would mean the lamp is standing on the table.

questions.prompt: I can't see the TV because my brother is standing right ---- it.
questions.explanationTR: 'In front of' means between you and the TV, so it blocks your view; someone 'behind' or 'next to' the TV would not stop you from seeing it.

questions.prompt: ---- any parking spaces on this street today?
questions.explanationTR: 'Parking spaces' is plural, and this is a question, so 'Are there' is correct; 'Is there' would need a singular noun, and 'There is/are' are not questions.

lessons.title: Gaps: a message to a neighbor

items.definition: a short note to a neighbor and seven questions about words for home and everyday problems

questions.prompt: Hi Mrs. Carter, I'm sorry, but there is a small ---- under my kitchen sink. Could you tell me who fixes things in the building?
questions.explanationTR: A 'leak' is a hole that lets water escape, which fits a plumbing problem under the sink; 'lease' is a rental agreement, not a physical problem.

questions.prompt: We just ---- last week, so we don't know many people in this building yet.
questions.explanationTR: 'Moved in' means started living in this new building, which matches not knowing the people here yet; 'moved away' describes leaving a place, not arriving at this one.

questions.prompt: Could I ---- your ladder for an hour? I need to change a light bulb in the kitchen.
questions.explanationTR: 'Borrow' means to take something and give it back later, which fits asking to use the neighbor's ladder for free; 'rent' would mean paying money for it, and 'lend' is used from the other person's point of view.

questions.prompt: Sorry for the noise last night - my apartment was very ---- because of the party.
questions.explanationTR: 'Noisy' means full of loud sound, which fits an apology about noise from a party; 'quiet' means the opposite.

questions.prompt: The collection truck comes early on Tuesdays, so please put your ---- out the night before.
questions.explanationTR: 'Garbage' is the waste that people put out for the collection truck; furniture, a lease, a view or a ceiling are not things you put out every week.

questions.prompt: Welcome to the building! I'm Lina from 4B, right next door. It's so nice to have a new ---- on our floor.
questions.explanationTR: A 'neighbor' is a person who lives next door, which is exactly what Lina describes; a 'roommate' shares your own apartment, not the one next door.

questions.prompt: The elevator is ---- again, so please use the stairs today.
questions.explanationTR: 'Broken' means not working, which explains why people should use the stairs instead; 'fixed' would mean it works fine.
